To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) protein motions in distal regions mediate similar active-site changes in the enzyme-substrate interaction during catalysis in homologous enzymes and in non-homolous enzymes that catalyze similar chemistry; (2) protein motions that are coupled to the chemical steps in enzyme mechanisms are conserved in homologous proteins across species and in non-hologous proteins that catalyze a common reaction.

1) The enzyme molecular architecture is conserved across species; 2) Enzymes are flexible molecules, and their flexibility is linked to enzyme catalysis; and 3) The reaction-coupled conformational changes of the enzyme molecular machinery are conserved across homologous and even non-homologus enzyme systems.
the protein function is intrinsically linked to its conformational flexibility, and the enzyme function (catalytic mechanism) is linked to its internal motions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolutionarily conserved linkage between enzyme fold, flexibility, and catalysis.
the identification and characterization, using detailed computational modeling, of the internal protein motion coupled to the chemical reaction step in enzyme catalysis.
the identification and characterization (using molecular dynamics) of the protein internal motions coupled to the catalyzed reaction in enzyme molecular architecture.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the conservation of enzyme structure and the conservation of the enzyme's internal motions are two sides of the same coin.
evolutionarily conserved enzyme fold, flexibility, and catalysis are intrinsically connected.
the enzyme flexibility is evolutionarily conserved and plays a crucial role in enzyme catalysis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
enzyme catalysis and protein flexibility are evolutionarily conserved.
the enzyme molecular architecture is designed to achieve the desired catalysis by the coupling of the reaction to the enzyme flexibility.
evolutionarily conserved protein flexibility is an essential component of enzyme catalysis, and that the protein flexibility is a consensual feature of the molecular architecture of the enzyme.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the enzyme flexibility is a conscribed feature of the molecular structure and function.
enzyme function is intimately linked to the protein flexibility, which in turn is linked to the protein structure.
the enzyme flexibility is conserved in nature and is a critical component of the enzyme molecular mechanism.
